title: Feedforward, Feedback, and System Status
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Feedforward, Feedback, and System Status. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedforward explains what can happen next: an action’s consequence, requirement, or availability. Feedback explains what happened after an action. System status explains the current state while work is ongoing or after it changes. Each reduces uncertainty at a different moment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design all three around the task. A destructive control needs feedforward; a completed upload needs feedback; a long-running export needs persistent status. Make messages durable when the consequence is durable, and keep the state visible where people will look for it later.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Explain possibility before action and reality after it
turns.text: What changes when we look at explain possibility before action and reality after it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedforward helps people predict what an action will do; feedback acknowledges input; status represents the resulting state over time. These functions are related but not interchangeable. A tooltip that predicts “Send request” cannot replace evidence that the service received it, and a success animation cannot justify a state the backend does not know.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: bank transfer?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Pay” needs feedforward about recipient, amount, fees, and timing. A spinner gives feedback. A receipt and transaction status provide evidence. Collapsing all three into a green tick can create serious false belief.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the action loop?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedforward explains what action is possible and what will happen. Feedback acknowledges input and shows resulting state. System status explains ongoing work, ownership, time, and next action. Together they let a person predict, act, interpret, and recover.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Match prominence and timing to consequence. Hover affordance is insufficient for touch and keyboard. A destructive control should name its effect before action. Immediate input needs acknowledgement within perceptual expectation; delayed work needs honest progress and the ability to continue elsewhere. Completion should state what changed, not merely say “Success.”

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Handle partial and uncertain states. Distinguish saved locally, synced, submitted, approved, and published. Announce dynamic changes to assistive technology without overwhelming. Avoid optimistic UI where a false success could cause costly repeat or loss.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Evaluate the complete loop by asking people to predict the result and explain current state. Errors often come from a broken transition, not a poorly drawn component.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build a status contract for every consequential action
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a status contract for every consequential action?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedforward appears before the boundary of commitment. The transfer review names clinic, information shared, protection of the existing appointment, and uncertainty. Feedback confirms that the system received input and prevents accidental repetition. Persistent status then shows the request object, latest trustworthy event, source, time, responsible actor, and next step.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Each layer answers a different question.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Latency is designed according to what the system knows. Short local work may need subtle inline feedback. Distributed review needs durable state and resumption. A timeout after submission becomes “checking whether your request was received,” not a confident failure and retry. Indeterminate progress is honest; fabricated percentages are not.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Notifications, in-product history, staff tools, and support share the event model. Out-of-order delivery, stale caches, partial failure, and background completion are tested. The team measures duplicate action, false belief, unresolved waiting, recovery, and support handoff. A delightful animation cannot compensate for an unsupported success claim.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: payment?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before payment, feedforward shows merchant, amount, fees, and timing. A pressed state acknowledges input. Authorisation, settlement, and refund are different statuses with different evidence. One green tick cannot safely represent all of them.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Transient confirmation is not adequate for consequential work. If a person must later prove what happened, preserve the evidence in the relevant object, history, or notification.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design feedback as a time sequence. Before action, make outcome, requirement, and reversibility visible. During work, show accepted, pending, blocked, or failed state and what the person can safely do. After work, preserve durable evidence when the outcome affects money, identity, publication, data, or another person.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Distinguish local acknowledgement from confirmed service completion.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: False completion: a toast implies success while the underlying operation is still pending or failed. Silent latency: people cannot tell whether to wait, retry, cancel, or seek help. Ephemeral receipt: consequential evidence disappears before it can be checked later. Status without action: a problem is displayed without a safe recovery route.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before pressing “Submit,” a person cannot tell whether they will send a draft or publish it. After pressing, the page flashes a toast but the status is unchanged. The system communicated neither consequence nor result reliably.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 148 protected work during creation. lesson 149 makes the system’s state and consequences legible. lesson 150 helps people learn a product without overwhelming them.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose one action in a product. Identify its feedforward, feedback, and lasting status. Add the missing piece if one is absent.
